summary.text: A stellar black hole is a black hole formed when a star collapses under its own gravity.
Its mass runs from about five to several tens of Suns, and a supernova explosion can leave one behind.
A collapsing star keeps crushing into a black hole when its mass is above the limit that neutron-degenerate matter can support.

facts.value: About five to several tens of Suns

facts.label: Only properties
facts.value: Mass, electric charge and angular momentum

facts.value: A 62-Sun black hole, found by gravitational waves in 2015

items.prompt: Three stars collapse at the end of their lives, with collapsing masses rising from small to very large. What do they leave, in that order?

options.label: Neutron star, white dwarf, black hole
Black hole, neutron star, white dwarf
White dwarf, neutron star, black hole
White dwarf, black hole, neutron star

items.explain: Below the Chandrasekhar limit a white dwarf results; above it but below the TOV limit, a neutron star; above the TOV limit, a black hole.

items.prompt: According to a famous theorem, which of these is NOT among a black hole's fundamental properties?

options.label: The chemical makeup of what fell in
Its total mass, taken as a whole
Its electric charge, if it has any
Its angular momentum, from the star's spin

items.explain: The no-hair theorem says a black hole can only have three fundamental properties: mass, electric charge and angular momentum.

items.prompt: A black hole and an ordinary star orbit each other closely. What lets astronomers detect the black hole?

options.label: The black hole's surface glows in visible light
Gas pulled from the star heats up and glows in X-rays
The black hole sends beams that sweep across Earth
The black hole shuts off the star's X-rays

items.explain: Matter transferred to the black hole heats to hundreds of millions of degrees and radiates in X-rays, while the companion is seen in optical telescopes.

items.prompt: A compact star in a binary weighs five times the Sun, more than any identified neutron star. Why do astronomers lean toward a black hole?

options.label: Neutron stars glow in X-rays but this one does not
Its orbit is too wide for a neutron star to hold on to
A neutron star cannot exist inside a binary system
No identified neutron star is that heavy, and no other object fits

items.explain: All identified neutron stars are below 3.0 solar masses, and astronomers can think of no other object for massive compact systems.

items.prompt: What would count as direct proof that a black hole exists?

options.label: Seeing a particle or gas cloud orbit as it falls in
Weighing it with X-ray and optical data
Seeing it glow in visible light
Counting the stars that circle around it

items.explain: Masses from X-ray and optical data are indirect; the direct proof would be observing the orbit of a particle or cloud falling into it.

items.prompt: Theory allows black holes of any mass, but no known stellar process makes one lighter than a few Suns. If one that light exists, where did it most likely come from?

options.label: It formed from a white dwarf shrinking
It is probably primordial, not made by a star
It was left by a planet crushed by a passing star
It formed from a neutron star slowly cooling

items.explain: No known stellar process yields black holes of a few solar masses or less; if they exist, they are most likely primordial.

paragraphs.heading: A black hole made by a star
paragraphs.text: A stellar black hole is a black hole made when a star collapses under its own gravity. Their masses run from about five to several tens of times the Sun's. Some are left over from supernova explosions, though other ways of forming them may also exist. A black hole can have only three basic properties: mass, electric charge and angular momentum, and a stellar black hole's angular momentum is carried over from the star or objects that made it.

paragraphs.heading: Which remnant forms
paragraphs.text: When a massive star has used up all its energy sources, its collapse cannot be avoided. If the collapsing part is under the Chandrasekhar limit, it becomes a white dwarf. If it is above that but under the Tolman–Oppenheimer–Volkoff (TOV) limit, it becomes a neutron star. Above the TOV limit the crushing goes on until a black hole forms. These limits are only approximate and may shift with the star's chemical makeup and spin.

paragraphs.heading: Where the line falls
paragraphs.text: The most a neutron star can weigh before collapsing into a black hole is not fully understood. In 1939 it was put at 0.7 solar masses, and a 1996 estimate put it between 1.5 and 3. The heaviest neutron star seen, PSR J0740+6620, found in 2019, is about 2.14 solar masses. General relativity allows black holes of any mass, but the smaller one is, the denser its matter must be, and no known process in stars makes black holes under a few solar masses.

paragraphs.heading: Record holders
paragraphs.text: Before 2016, the biggest stellar black hole on record had 15.65±1.45 solar masses. In September 2015, gravitational waves revealed a spinning black hole of 62±4 solar masses forming as two smaller black holes merged. In 2020, the smallest black hole known was reported in the binary system 2MASS J05215658+4359220, at 3.3 solar masses and just 19.5 kilometers across.

paragraphs.heading: Seeing the invisible
paragraphs.text: In a close binary, matter flowing from a companion star falls toward the black hole and heats to several hundred million degrees, glowing in X-rays. So the black hole shows up in X-rays, while the companion can be seen with optical telescopes. Neutron stars release about as much energy, so the two are often hard to tell apart. But every identified neutron star is under 3.0 solar masses, and no compact system above that shows neutron star traits, so the heavier ones look more and more likely to be black holes.
